snip.t: A normal blood pressure does not rule out shock; hypotension (systolic blood pressure $<90\text{ mmHg}$ or mean arterial pressure $<65\text{ mmHg}$) is a late manifestation of vascular decompensation.
Bedside screen (qSOFA): two or more of respiratory rate 22 or more, altered mentation, systolic blood pressure 100 or less.
Pulse pressure = systolic blood pressure minus diastolic blood pressure.
snip.s: Approach to Cardiovascular Symptoms and Examination

snip.t: 1. *Shock:* Systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg, pallor, cold extremities, diaphoresis.
Pulsus paradoxus: An exaggerated inspiratory drop in systolic blood pressure (>10 mmHg).
Persistent resting tachycardia, hypotension (systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg), or refractory fluid overload.

Vasodilators: If systolic blood pressure remains adequate, start an intravenous nitrate infusion (glyceryl trinitrate) to unload the left ventricle by reducing systemic vascular resistance and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.
Hypotension: Systolic blood pressure $<90\text{ mmHg}$ or mean arterial pressure $<65\text{ mmHg}$ indicates failure of compensatory vasoconstriction to offset low stroke volume or vasodilation.

qs.q: A 32-year-old man involved in a motor vehicle collision presents with a penetrating abdominal injury and active haemorrhage. His systolic blood pressure is 85 mmHg and mean arterial pressure is 55 mmHg. What is the primary clinical rationale for avoiding immediate aggressive crystalloid normalisation of his blood pressure?
o: To prevent disruption of an immature platelet-fibrin clot
To ensure complete cessation of bleeding without surgery
To eliminate the risk of transfusion-related acute lung injury
To maintain normal renal perfusion and prevent kidney failure
qs.e: Permissive hypotension avoids high pressure that can disrupt early clots and dilute coagulation factors. It is a temporary bridge, not a definitive replacement for surgical control.

qs.q: An adult trauma patient without a traumatic brain injury is being managed with hypotensive resuscitation while awaiting emergency laparotomy for an intra-abdominal bleed. Which of the following represents the commonly cited temporary systolic blood pressure target?
o: Target a temporary systolic blood pressure of 60 to 70 mmHg
Target a temporary systolic blood pressure of 100 to 110 mmHg
Target a temporary systolic blood pressure of 120 to 130 mmHg
Target a temporary systolic blood pressure of 80 to 90 mmHg
qs.e: In selected adult trauma patients without traumatic brain injury, the commonly cited temporary SBP target is approximately 80-90 mmHg. Higher pressures may worsen bleeding before definitive control.

qs.q: An investigator wants to visually inspect the linear association between patient age and systolic blood pressure using paired numerical coordinates. Which Excel or SPSS chart type is most appropriate?
o: Pie proportion ring
Column bar chart
Line trend series
Scatter plot graph
Area density map
qs.e: A scatter plot displays the relationship between two continuous variables.

qs.q: To test whether a new antihypertensive reduces systolic blood pressure more than standard therapy, which design provides the strongest evidence?
o: Case-control observational study design
Randomized controlled clinical trial design
Cross-sectional survey observational design
Prospective cohort observational study design
qs.e: A randomised controlled trial minimizes bias by allocating participants to interventions randomly. The other designs are more prone to confounding.

qs.q: An emergency physician examines a patient experiencing a severe asthma exacerbation and notes a fall in systolic blood pressure of 14 mmHg during inspiration. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism causing this finding?
o: Exaggerated negative intrathoracic pressure increasing right-heart venous return and shifting the septum into the left ventricle
Acute pulmonary embolism causing sudden mechanical obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract during inspiration
Systemic vasodilation secondary to intravenous magnesium sulphate administration during emergency care management
Direct suppression of myocardial contractility by circulating inflammatory mediators released from mucosal mast cells
qs.e: Pulsus paradoxus is caused by exaggerated negative intrathoracic pressure increasing venous return to the right heart, shifting the interventricular septum, and decreasing left ventricular stroke volume. It is not caused by direct myocardial suppression or pulmonary embolism.
qs.s: Bronchial Asthma: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis and GINA Stepwise: MCQs

qs.q: An adult patient with severe asthma is assessed in the emergency department. The clinician records a fall in systolic blood pressure during inspiration exceeding 10 mmHg. What is the correct term for this physical finding and its implication?
o: Pulsus paradoxus, indicating a severe asthma exacerbation
Paradoxical pulse, indicating primary left ventricular overload
Kussmaul sign, indicating right ventricular heart failure
Pulsus alternans, indicating severe left ventricular dysfunction
qs.e: A pulsus paradoxus greater than 10 mmHg is a sign of severe asthma caused by large swings in intrathoracic pressure affecting venous return and cardiac output. It reflects profound airflow limitation and increased work of breathing.
qs.s: Bronchial Asthma: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis and GINA Stepwise: MCQs

qs.q: A 54-year-old man in the ICU is noted to have a pulse of 35 beats per minute and a systolic blood pressure of 85 mmHg following an emergency laparotomy. Which of the following parameters represents an explicit severity trigger for ICU admission?
o: Respiratory rate of 12 breaths per minute
Oxygen saturation of 94% on room air
Systolic blood pressure under 90 mmHg
Pulse rate of 35 beats per minute
qs.e: A systolic blood pressure under 90 mmHg is an explicit severity trigger for ICU admission. A pulse under 40 is a trigger, making the 35 bpm value slightly outside the exact stated threshold of 'under 40' though clinically similar, but the hypotension is explicitly listed as under 90 mmHg.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a motor‑vehicle crash. He is hypotensive with a systolic blood pressure of 85 mmHg and has a severe head injury with a GCS of 6. What is the most appropriate initial conclusion about his hypotension?
o: He is probably experiencing neurogenic shock from brainstem injury.
His low blood pressure is most likely caused by raised intracranial pressure.
His fluid resuscitation should initially avoid isotonic crystalloids.
He should be presumed to have occult hemorrhage until proven otherwise.
qs.e: In polytrauma, hypotension is assumed to be due to extracranial bleeding until a source is identified, because hemorrhage is the most common reversible cause. Neurogenic shock is uncommon after isolated head injury and does not typically produce such profound hypotension.
